newsitem.title: KENYA: Conservationist says trade in ivory dangerous.
newsitem.headline: Conservationist says trade in ivory dangerous.

text.p: Elephant conservationist Iain Douglas-Hamilton on Friday described as dangerous a campaign by Namibia, Zimbabwe and Botswana to allow limited trade in ivory.

Douglas-Hamilton, of conservation organisation Save the Elephants, said that reopening the ivory trade would send the wrong signal to the world that elephant populations had miraculously recovered, trading was legitimate again and that poaching was profitable and worth the risk.
"It would stimulate demand and increase the incentive for poaching. By contrast a continued ban would...stifle demand for ivory and keep the price of ivory at unprofitable levels.
"A limited trade it is said would be to everyone's benefit including the elephants. These are dangerous perceptions. These arguments are fatally flawed," he said.

Douglas-Hamilton is chairman of the board of trustees of the Nairobi-based Save the Elephants. He issued a statement in Kenya ahead of the Convention for International Trade and Endangered Species (CITES) in the Zimbabwean capital Harare next week.

Douglas-Hamilton said Save the Elephants joined Kenya in strongly opposing downlisting of African elephants from Appendix I to Appendix II that allows ivory trade since it would "inevitably catalyse a parallel illegal trade and result in ivory poaching which will quickly spiral out of control".

He said recent evidence of illegal trade involving Zimbabwe, South Africa, Hong Kong, Japan and Taiwan indicated that substantial demand for ivory existed and that these countries did not have mechanisms to control illegal trade.

He said small gains to southern African countries from ivory trade were trivial compared to their overall economies and would be greatly outweighed by the cost other countries -- especially East Africa -- would have to pay for increased law enforcement.

He said that while the ban cut demand in the West and Japan, new potentially devastating markets were emerging in China, Hong Kong, Taiwan, Thailand, South Korea and demand in these nations dwarfed the effect of Japanese demand in the 1970s and 1980s.

He rejected suggestions that local people would benefit from ivory trade: "At best money has been swallowed up by the central government treasuries but usually it has been only crooked ivory traders or poachers who have benefited. Commerce in ivory has typically been surrounded by corruption."

More than half of Africa's elephant population was wiped out by ivory trade in 1979 to 1989. In the 1980s, international ivory trade averaged 700 tonnes annually or the slaughter of 70,000 elephants, only 20 percent of these legal, according to Save the Elephant figures.

Total loss of elephants in Eastern Africa from 1977 to 1989 was 74 percent or 185,000 elephants and included massive drops in populations in Kenya, Uganda, Tanzania, Cameroon, Chad, Central African Republic, former Zaire, Sudan and Somalia, Save the Elephant added.
Zambia, Mozambique and Angola also saw declines in elephant populations while Zimbabwe, Botswana, Namibia and South Africa saw stable or increasing elephant herds, it said.
Douglas-Hamilton did not give figures for elephant recoveries around Africa in the period after 1989.
